extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and illustrative examples for applying the two-step subject-matter eligibility (35 U.S.C. §101 / Alice) analysis to business-method and software-implemented claims. Explains how to identify abstract ideas and when additional claim elements amount to an 'inventive concept' (significantly more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory category (machine/process/etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category of invention (e.g., process, machine). The examples check Step 1 first (e.g., the claim is a process or a machine) and record Step 1: Yes when satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify claim recites a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition). This is the threshold procedural check before determining whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: Is the claim directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (e.g., fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, or mental processes). Example: fraud prevention by verifying a customer's identity is characterized as a long‑prevalent business practice and thus an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to the language of the claim that describes the abstract concept (e.g., obtaining and comparing customer information, inventory management, data collection and storage). Compare claim concept to ideas courts have previously found abstract (e.g., intermediated settlement, risk hedging, content extraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Does the claim recite 'significantly more' (an inventive concept)?
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying an abstract idea, analyze whether any element or combination of elements transforms the claim into a patent-eligible application by providing significantly more than the abstract idea (an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider additional limitations individually and in combination. Identify whether the limitations are conventional/generic or whether they represent a specific, non‑conventional and non‑generic implementation that improves a technical field (citing Diehr, Bascom, DDR as positive examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional or generic computer components do not supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that recite generic computer elements (e.g., a processor, memory, a programmed computer, a mobile communication device) or routine functions (reading data, generating random codes, comparing data) are considered well‑understood, routine, conventional activities and do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When components are recited at a high level of generality and merely perform typical programmed functions (storing, processing, comparing), treat them as generic computer implementations that do not confer eligibility (Step 2B: No).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere automation of a longstanding business practice is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely automate a mental or economic practice (e.g., verification steps previously performed mentally by tellers) do not provide significantly more than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why automation is no more than the sum of conventional parts performing routine functions. Emphasize that mere automation of economic/business practice is not an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere selection or manipulation of particular information is still abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting the selection, manipulation, or storage of particular information (e.g., images, classification and location data) does not make an otherwise abstract concept patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Electric Power Group and Digitech: selecting and manipulating particular information by itself does not make an abstract concept less abstract. The use of a programmed computer as a tool to perform these tasks generally does not supply significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant pre‑solution activity / mere data gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim steps that are high-level data gathering (e.g., obtaining customer-specific information from a bank card) may be considered insignificant pre-solution activity and not contribute to an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label obvious data-collection steps as mere inputs necessary to use the abstract idea rather than technical improvements. Such steps, when recited at a high level, usually do not transform the claim into eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑conventional combination or sequence can provide an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of conventional elements may provide significantly more if the combination operates in a non‑conventional and non‑generic way to solve a technical problem (e.g., sequence of ATM random code, mobile-device generated encrypted-image, ATM decryption/analysis to prevent skimmed card fraud).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed combination sets up a specific sequence of events or a particular technical implementation that addresses unique problems and differs from routine/conventional sequences (Bascom/DDR style reasoning). If so, treat the combination as a practical implementation that can supply 'significantly more' (Step 2B: Yes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims focused on specific improvements in computer functionality (Enfish) may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to a specific improvement in how a computer operates or a technological improvement in computer functionality can be patent-eligible, even if implemented on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish claims that improve computer functionality (Enfish) from claims that merely use computers as tools. If the claim's focus is a technological improvement in computer behavior, that can weigh in favor of eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting/docketing practice: clarify reasons for eligibility or ineligibility in the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Although an examiner is not required to provide an explanation of eligibility, the record is enhanced if clarifying remarks are provided to point to the reason for eligibility or to explain why additional limitations are conventional when rejecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is eligible, point to the combination of elements used in the non‑conventional implementation. If rejecting, identify the abstract idea and explain why additional limitations are conventional or generic (e.g., why a processor or memory performs only routine functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation: give broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: For recently filed applications under examination, claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain meaning of claim terms unless the specification provides special definitions. This interpretive standard affects whether limitations are read narrowly enough to supply an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare to precedent when characterizing abstractness or inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedents (e.g., Alice, CyberSource, Diehr, Bascom, Enfish, Electric Power, DDR, Content Extraction, TLI Communications, Digitech) to determine whether a claim's idea is similar to concepts previously found abstract or whether limitations are analogous to prior eligible claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state which case(s) the claim is similar to and why (e.g., similarity to CyberSource for obtaining/comparing intangible data for fraud detection). Use precedential analogies to justify Step 2A or Step 2B conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventory-management and imaging claims: evaluate as data-collection/recognition concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite capturing images, extracting features (character and contour), forming feature vectors, classifying, tracking across overlapping cameras, reconstructing 3‑D coordinates, and updating inventory records are analyzed as concepts of data collection/recognition and may be directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such claims merely use generic cameras, models, and processors for recognition/tracking without a specific technical improvement in imaging/computer vision, treat them as abstract (Step 2A) and evaluate additional limitations for conventionality. Show why memory/processor recitations are generic and do not supply an inventive concept unless they amount to a specific technological improvement.
